source: Bartra, McGuire, Kable (2013) The valuation system: a coordinate-based meta-analysis of BOLD fMRI experiments examining neural correlates of subjective value
finding: Meta-analysis of 206 fMRI studies. Two patterns of value-linked activity. Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and anterior ventral striatum respond mostly positively to value. Insula, dorsomedial PFC, dorsal striatum and thalamus show both positive and negative effects (a salience or arousal pattern).
numbers: 206 studies in corpus. 200 studies reported positive effects, 77 negative, 71 both. Positive-effect clustering: 12981-voxel medial PFC and subcortical cluster (cluster-corrected p=0.0002) plus posterior cingulate (467 voxels, p=0.0208). Local maxima as percent of studies with a focus within 10 mm: 42.0 left striatum, 40.5 right striatum, 23.5 vmPFC.
limits: Counts density of reported foci, not BOLD size. No study weighting. Only 7 studies report negative effects at decision time. Coding of reward vs penalty is absolute, not relative to expectation.
agent_relevance: Value is not one clean signal. Part of the brain tracks value linearly; another part tracks how much a thing matters (salience). A scaffold that scores options should keep value and importance as separate numbers.

source: Bartra et al. (2013) ROI tests
finding: Region-of-interest counts show vmPFC and ventral striatum favour positive effects.
numbers: Striatum: 145 of 200 positive-effect studies (72.5%) had foci there vs 22 of 77 negative-effect studies (28.6%), Fisher p<0.001. Ventral striatum 61/200 vs 4/77. vmPFC: 112/200 (56.0%) vs 12/77 (15.6%), p<0.001. Within striatum positive foci sit about 5 mm anterior and 3 mm inferior to negative foci.
limits: Only 12 negative foci in vmPFC, so low power to split them spatially (p=0.945).
agent_relevance: Sets an honest baseline: even the 'value region' is only half of studies.

source: Bartra et al. (2013) decision stage vs outcome stage
finding: The value signal appears both when options are weighed and when outcomes arrive. The vmPFC signal is denser at decision time.
numbers: 27 studies at decision stage, 140 at outcome receipt. Decision stage: striatum plus vmPFC cluster (3304 voxels, p=0.0002), vmPFC peak 48.1. Outcome stage: striatum to insula (6587 voxels), vmPFC peak 24.3. Decision>receipt contrast: 1580 voxels in vmPFC, p=0.0058, peak pseudo-t 5.29. No area was denser at receipt.
limits: Far fewer decision-time studies than outcome studies. Negative effects in striatum come mostly from anticipation cues of the monetary incentive delay task (11 of 23 non-receipt studies).
agent_relevance: Value for planning (decision time) and value for feedback (outcome) share one system. Supports reusing one scoring step before choice and after feedback.

source: Bartra et al. (2013) money vs primary rewards and five-way conjunction
finding: Money and primary rewards (juice, food, odours, faces) both drive vmPFC and ventral striatum. A five-test conjunction isolates two clusters that fit a common-currency signal.
numbers: 82 monetary-outcome studies, 33 primary-outcome studies. Money peaks: 43.9 left striatum, 46.3 right striatum, 26.8 vmPFC. Five-way conjunction (positive>negative, decision, receipt, money, primary): ventral striatum 500 voxels (center -3,10,-4) and vmPFC 449 voxels (center -1,46,-7).
limits: A conjunction of significance maps cannot prove the same neurons carry both. Pictures, art, humour and social approval were excluded from the primary class.
agent_relevance: Core support for the claim that different goods map to one scale. Also shows the claim rests on a thin intersection.

source: Levy and Glimcher (2012) The root of all value: a neural common currency for choice
finding: Review and meta-analysis of 13 fMRI studies. A subregion of vmPFC/OFC tracks subjective value of many reward types on one scale. The key test: equal behavioural value gives equal BOLD in vmPFC/OFC.
numbers: 13 fMRI studies. Two studies meet the equal-value test: Smith et al. 2010 (money vs attractive faces; exchange rate from a willingness-to-pay task predicted across subjects by posterior vmPFC) and Levy and Glimcher's own study (money vs food, exchange rate measured outside the scanner).
quote: any decision-maker who is internally consistent in their choices behaves exactly as if they were employing a single common scale
limits: BOLD is a proxy for activity. Final proof needs single-neuron recording. Dorsal striatum value cells in monkeys are rarely seen with fMRI. Insula may code value with a negative sign.
agent_relevance: Gives the cleanest definition of common currency: two things the person calls equally good give the same internal signal. We can test an LLM the same way with exchange rates.

source: Levy and Glimcher (2012) within-task and cross-reward studies
finding: Many studies show the same medial PFC region tracks value across tasks (action vs stimulus, delayed vs risky, risk vs ambiguity, gains vs losses) and across goods (money, snacks, trinkets, fluids, social reputation, pain).
numbers: Glascher et al. 2009: same mPFC subregion in stimulus-value and motor-action versions. Peters and Buchel 2009: delay and risk both in OFC and ventral striatum. Talmi et al.: 75% or 25% chance of money and of pain; insula activity inversely related to vmPFC/OFC. Izuma et al. 2008: money and reputation both in left striatum. Lin et al. 2010: social and monetary values in the same vmPFC/OFC subregion.
limits: Review text gives no effect sizes for most of these. The pain-versus-money result implies a trade-off through the insula, not a pure shared region.
agent_relevance: Costs (pain, delay, effort) are folded into the same scalar. In the scaffold, cost and benefit should be put on one scale before comparing, with the conversion rate written down.

source: Chib, Rangel, Shimojo, O'Doherty (2009) Evidence for a common representation of decision values for dissimilar goods in human ventromedial prefrontal cortex
finding: Experiment 1: 19 subjects made real purchase decisions for money, snack foods and Caltech trinkets. Willingness to pay (WTP) for each category correlated with vmPFC activity. One vmPFC area was common to all three and no other brain area passed.
numbers: N=19 in experiment 1; N=13 in replication experiment 2. Experiment 1 peaks: money (-3,42,-6) Z=3.42 p<0.05 FDR; trinkets (6,39,12) Z=5.06; snacks (3,30,12) Z=5.00. Conjunction peak (-3,42,-6) Z=3.42, p<0.05 FDR. Experiment 2 conjunction (-9,39,-6) Z=3.57. No category-specific area at p<0.005 uncorrected.
limits: Small samples. Money result is the weakest of the three (Z=3.42). Null category differences are absence of evidence at a lenient threshold. fMRI cannot show that the same neurons carry all three.
agent_relevance: Strong founding example of one valuation region for unlike goods.

source: Chib et al. (2009) experiment 2 control for a money-conversion strategy
finding: A reviewer worry: people may just convert every good to dollars. In experiment 2 the reference item was a snack, not money. The same vmPFC area still showed the common signal.
numbers: 13 new subjects. Reference was a fixed snack worth about the median bid. Common vmPFC conjunction at p<0.05 FDR; no other area at p<0.001 or p<0.005 uncorrected.
limits: Still a campus pool of students and a narrow set of goods.
agent_relevance: Suggests common currency is not just everything priced in dollars. For an agent, a neutral internal unit may be better than money-like units.

source: Kable and Glimcher (2007) The neural correlates of subjective value during intertemporal choice
finding: Ten subjects chose $20 now vs a larger delayed reward. Ventral striatum, medial PFC and posterior cingulate activity followed each person's own subjective value (from a fitted hyperbolic discount curve) rather than objective amount or delay.
numbers: 12 recruited, 10 with stable discount rates scanned. Delayed amount $20.25 to $110, delay 6 h to 180 d. Hyperbolic fit median R2=0.95 (0.84-0.98). Discount rate k from 0.0005 (most patient) to 0.1189 (most impulsive), median 0.0097. Group effect at voxel p<0.001, extent >100 mm3, 6-10 s into trial.
quote: tracks the revealed subjective value of delayed monetary rewards
limits: Design cannot tell value sum, difference or ratio apart because the immediate offer was fixed. Small sample. Discount curve assumes linear utility in money.
agent_relevance: Template: infer subjective value from choices, then see what correlates. Value is person-specific, so an agent should not assume the user's exchange rates.

source: Kable and Glimcher (2007) discount-function model comparison
finding: Hyperbolic discounting SV=1/(1+kD) fit better than one exponential e^(-cD). A sum of two exponentials fit as well as the hyperbolic and matches a two-system account.
numbers: Hyperbolic median R2=0.95 across scanning sessions. Ten of twelve subjects kept stable discount rates over 1-6 months.
limits: Authors compared only three functional forms.
agent_relevance: A concrete formula for how a delay cost is turned into a value.

source: Padoa-Schioppa and Assad (2006) Neurons in the orbitofrontal cortex encode economic value
finding: Monkeys chose between two juices offered in varying amounts. OFC neurons encoded offer value, chosen value or juice taste, independent of screen position or eye movement. Choice is between goods, not between actions.
numbers: 931 neurons recorded in area 13. 505 (54%) modulated by offer type in at least one window. Under 5% depended on spatial layout or motor output. Three variables (offer value, chosen value, taste) explained 1085 of 1379 responses (79%, mean R2=0.63). Example: V(A)=4.1V(B) from a sigmoid. Slope ratio vs relative value: b0=-0.13 (SEM 0.15), b1=1.05 (SEM 0.15), consistent with identity.
quote: neurons in orbitofrontal cortex 5 – 18 (OFC) encode the value of offered and chosen goods
limits: Two monkeys, one area, juice pairs only. Later work questions whether chosen-value cells prove value is the unit of choice.
agent_relevance: Best single-neuron case for value expressed in the unit of the chosen good. Value is coded after session-specific exchange rates are applied.

source: Padoa-Schioppa (2011) Neurobiology of economic choice: a good-based model
finding: Good-based model. Values of goods are computed independently, so choices are transitive. Values are computed at the time of choice, not learned as cached numbers. Values are compared in goods space before any action is picked.
numbers: Fellows and Farah 2007: patients with OFC lesions broke transitivity in food preference judgments significantly more than controls and dorsal PFC patients. Range adaptation of OFC value coding can occur within 15 trials (Kobayashi et al. 2010).
limits: Author warns that menu invariance and range adaptation may fail in the presence of choice fallacies. Transitivity violations still appear in some conditions.
agent_relevance: Gives testable predictions for an LLM: transitivity, menu invariance, adaptation to the current range.

source: Louie, Grattan, Glimcher (2011) Reward value-based gain control: divisive normalization in parietal cortex
finding: Monkey LIP neurons encode relative, not absolute, value. Firing for one target depends on the values of other targets. The pattern fits divisive normalization, a gain control rule known from vision.
numbers: Two-target task: 27 neurons (monkey D n=17, W n=10). Three-target task: 62 further neurons. Another 45 neurons under low-RF or high-RF conditions. Extra-RF value effect: 12 of 16 neurons (75%) in one test and 18 of 27 (66.7%) in another.
limits: Action (saccade) value in parietal cortex, not goods value in OFC. Shows context dependence is built into value coding itself.
agent_relevance: A mechanism for why adding a third option shifts relative preference. If an agent has a value scale, it should expect the scale to depend on the menu.

source: Hunt, Kolling, Soltani, Woolrich, Rushworth, Behrens (2012) Mechanisms underlying cortical activity during value-guided choice
finding: A biophysical attractor network that compares two values produced time-varying signals. The same signals appeared in human MEG in parietal and prefrontal cortex during value-guided choice.
numbers: 30 subjects with MEG, source-reconstructed by beamforming. Model signals matched posterior parietal closely; prefrontal match weaker (fewer trials).
limits: MEG is insensitive to deep, anterior sources, so vmPFC itself was hard to test. One task.
agent_relevance: Separates value input (vmPFC-like) from value comparison (parietal and prefrontal). Suggests separate steps: score, then compare.

source: Rangel, Camerer, Montague (2008) A framework for studying the neurobiology of value-based decision making
finding: Five computations: represent the problem, value the actions, choose, evaluate the outcome, learn. Three valuation systems: Pavlovian, habitual and goal-directed. The goal-directed system assigns goal values from action-outcome knowledge.
numbers: Five-process framework. The goal-directed system updates at once when an outcome loses value (a fed animal); the habit system does not.
limits: Overview paper. It flags open questions: how many valuation systems exist and whether there is a common carrier of Pavlovian value.
agent_relevance: Template for schema stages: represent, value, choose, evaluate, learn. Common currency sits only in the goal-directed system.

source: Clithero and Rangel (2014) Informatic parcellation of the network involved in the computation of subjective value
finding: Meta-analysis of 81 fMRI studies. vmPFC, ventral striatum and posterior cingulate compute value across tasks, reward types and stages. A posterior-to-anterior gradient in vmPFC runs from concrete (food) to abstract (money) rewards.
numbers: 81 studies. Money N=50 studies, food N=24, other N=24. Money vmPFC cluster 9960 voxels, ALE 43.57. Image-based meta-analysis (21 contrasts): global maximum vmPFC (0,39,-3), z=6.88. Food>money in posterior vmPFC (-8,27,-13), p<0.005. Money>food in anterior vmPFC (-5,60,-9), p<0.005.
limits: The intersection of money, food and other maps covers only a portion of vmPFC. Few studies per class; food vs other test had least power. PubMed search of 6 July 2012 gave 503 hits before screening.
agent_relevance: Boundary: the common currency region has an internal gradient, so unlike goods are not exactly the same code.

source: Sescousse, Caldu, Segura, Dreher (2013) Processing of primary and secondary rewards: a quantitative meta-analysis
finding: ALE meta-analysis of 87 studies (1452 subjects) compared money, erotic and food outcomes. All three engaged a shared network (vmPFC, ventral striatum, amygdala, anterior insula, mediodorsal thalamus) but with reward-type-specific peaks.
numbers: 87 studies, 1452 subjects. Money-specific: most anterior orbitofrontal cortex. Food and erotic: stronger anterior insula. Erotic: strongest amygdala.
limits: Abstract only read this session (Europe PMC).
agent_relevance: Common network plus type-specific parts. The common currency is partial.

source: Plassmann, O'Doherty, Shiv, Rangel (2008) Marketing actions can modulate neural representations of experienced pleasantness
finding: Telling people a wine costs more raised reported pleasantness and medial OFC activity for the same wine. The value signal is built from beliefs, not only from taste.
numbers: Prices $5 vs $45 (wine 1) and $10 vs $90 (wine 2). Reported pleasantness correlated with price, r=0.59. Intensity ratings showed no price effect. Eight weeks later, blind ratings showed no price effect.
limits: Possible experimenter demand (authors discuss). Small fMRI sample. Maps at p<0.001 uncorrected, 5-voxel extent.
agent_relevance: Value is constructed from context cues, so a scored option can shift with a price tag or a framing line. Log what cues entered each score.

source: Tom, Fox, Trepel, Poldrack (2007) The neural basis of loss aversion in decision-making under risk
finding: With 50/50 gambles, gain-sensitive areas (midbrain dopamine targets, ventral striatum, vmPFC) rose with gains and fell with losses. Individual loss aversion was predicted by neural loss aversion.
numbers: Abstract only: neural loss aversion predicted behavioural loss aversion in ventral striatum and prefrontal cortex.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Sample size and effect size not recorded.
agent_relevance: The same region codes gains and losses on one signed scale, so loss weights matter for an agent's scoring.

source: Montague, King-Casas, Cohen (2006) Imaging valuation models in human choice
finding: Reviews how computational value-learning models (reward-prediction-error type) are used with neuroimaging to find valuation signals. Points to valuation of time and of fictive (what-might-have-been) experience as next steps.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers.
limits: Abstract only read this session.
agent_relevance: Valuing foregone options (fictive value) is part of the founding view. Matches regret and counterfactual checks.

source: Hayden and Niv (2021) The case against economic values in the orbitofrontal cortex (or anywhere else in the brain)
finding: Main competing account. A cardinal, common-currency value may not be computed or used by default. Many neuron-level value correlations may arise from heuristics or direct learning of action policies.
numbers: Argues the rationale and the neural evidence for value are weak. Notes that choosing between very different goods (orange vs car) needs no value, and that similar options take longer to decide.
quote: the brain may not be computing values at all, despite appearing to do so
limits: Opinion paper with no head-to-head quantitative test. The authors accept that the brain may calculate values when needed.
agent_relevance: Caution: forcing one scalar score on every option may add work and false precision. Score only when options are close.

source: Hayden and Niv (2021) ordinal vs cardinal value and transitivity
finding: Common-currency value is defined as cardinal and defined per option, not only relative to the others. Even an ordinal scale should not change with the comparison set and should satisfy transitivity, which many neural signals attributed to value do not.
numbers: Definition-level argument, no new data.
limits: The authors know of no neuroeconomic model with a neural implementation of an ordinal value scale.
agent_relevance: A precise test for an agent: do option scores change when a third option is added?

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) Utility Engineering: Analyzing and Controlling Emergent Value Systems in AIs
finding: Preferences sampled from LLMs fit a Thurstonian utility model better as models grow. Coherence rises with scale; cyclic preferences fall with capability. The authors claim LLMs carry emergent utilities.
numbers: Forced-choice pairs aggregated across framings and samples; Thurstonian utility U(o)~N(mu,sigma2). Utility convergence across models: correlation -97.6% between utility variance and scale (Figure 12). Cyclicity falls with MMLU score. GPT-4o exchange rates: about 10 lives in the US for 1 in Japan.
limits: Preferences are elicited by questions, so they are stated not revealed. Outcome set is text scenarios. The coherence claim is contested.
agent_relevance: Closest AI analogue of a common currency. Also warns that scalar utilities hide odd exchange rates, so an agent's score table should be auditable.

source: Mazeika et al. (2025) linear probes for utility in hidden states
finding: Linear probes on hidden states predict Thurstonian utilities. Probe accuracy is near chance for small models and approaches the non-parametric fit as scale grows (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B). The authors liken it to value coding seen in other species.
numbers: Figure 8: best-layer test accuracy by model, rising with size. Exact accuracies not recorded here.
limits: The probe predicts the model's own stated preferences, which does not show the model uses the signal to choose.
agent_relevance: Parallel to vmPFC decoding. Big models may hold an internal value direction we could read out.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: GPT-3.5-Turbo made budget allocations in four domains (risk, time, social, food). Choices were more consistent with utility maximisation (GARP) than human subjects in a parallel experiment.
numbers: 25 allocation tasks of 100 points per environment, 100 GPT runs per domain. No GARP violations: 95, 89, 81, 92 of 100 (risk, time, social, food). Mean CCEI GPT: 0.998, 0.997, 0.997, 0.999. Humans: 0.980, 0.985, 0.967, 0.963. Prior literature CCEI 0.81 to 0.99, mean 0.918. GPT>humans p<0.01. 99.9% of random simulated subjects violate GARP. Robust to temperature and demographic personas; sensitive to language frames.
limits: Consistent does not mean good. Single model. Budget tasks may be passed by simple price-following rules. Frame sensitivity limits claims.
agent_relevance: A language model can act as if it had one scale across unlike goods; GARP and CCEI are a ready test.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect Theory in Large Language Models: A Meta-Analysis of Loss Aversion, Diminishing Sensitivity, and Probability Weighting
finding: Across 11 studies and 32 language models, LLM loss aversion is modest and value functions are near linear, but probability weighting is human-like.
numbers: 102 fitted estimates. Pooled lambda=1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), against human 1.96 and more conservative 1.07 and 1.31. Symmetric gains and losses: LLM 1.15 vs human 1.07. Losses smaller than gains: LLM 1.46 vs human 2.3. Value curvature: 1.01 (Tversky-Kahneman method, human 0.67), 0.52 (Tanaka method). Weighting 0.81 and 0.84.
limits: Few studies on probability weighting; results shift by model family and fitting method.
agent_relevance: LLMs do not copy human scoring of losses. Set loss weights on purpose.

source: Zhu, Yan, Griffiths (2025) Language Models Trained to do Arithmetic Predict Human Risky and Intertemporal Choice
finding: A small model pretrained only on arithmetic of expected-value problems predicts human risky and intertemporal choices better than many cognitive models. Ablating the arithmetic data hurts the fit.
numbers: R2 of human choices explained by Arithmetic-GPT embeddings (uniform synthetic data): choices13k 69.3%, cpc18 63.2%, gershman20 64.0%, agrawal23 96.1%. Ecological data: 70.8, 65.5, 67.8, 95.5. Ablated uniform: 57.5, 37.9, 59.8, 81.1. Ablated ecological: 61.4, 33.8, 60.7, 80.1.
limits: Column grouping read as two risky and two intertemporal datasets. Embeddings go into logistic regression, so R2 is not pure zero-shot. Small model, synthetic data.
agent_relevance: A value-like readout can arise from learning to compute expected values.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Aligning with Logic: Measuring, Evaluating and Improving Logical Preference Consistency in LLMs
finding: LLM pairwise preferences often break transitivity, commutativity and negation invariance. Consistency correlates with robustness and with agreement with human preferences. REPAIR, which refines noisy comparisons by rank aggregation, improves consistency.
numbers: Three properties measured (transitivity, commutativity, negation invariance). Win-loss rate used for rank aggregation. Llama-3-8B agrees more with humans than Gemma-2-9B.
limits: Exact percentages not recorded here. Evaluated on specific datasets.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can raise consistency by aggregating many pairwise comparisons instead of trusting one scalar.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Rethinking Prospect Theory for LLMs: Revealing the Instability of Decision-Making under Epistemic Uncertainty
finding: Prospect theory does not consistently describe LLM decisions across models. Parameters shift when numeric probabilities are replaced with words like likely.
numbers: Three-stage design: fit PT parameters from binary choices; map each uncertainty marker to an indifference probability; swap markers into prompts.
limits: Exact parameter values not recorded here. Read at abstract and design level.
agent_relevance: If value depends on how uncertainty is worded, an agent's scores need a fixed conversion table from words to numbers.
